extracted.intended_audience: critics, reviewers, and educated readers assessing scientific or philosophical criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for judging the validity of a critic's verdicts by examining their habitual mental traits, methodological consistency, command of abstractions, use of examples, and domain-appropriateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study a critic's mental peculiarities
rubrics_metrics.description: One way of estimating the validity of a critic's judgments is that of studying his mental peculiarities as generally displayed. If he betrays idiosyncrasies of thought in his writings at large, it may be inferred that these idiosyncrasies possibly, if not probably, give a character to the verdicts he passes upon the productions of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspect the critic's other writings and habitual modes of thinking. If recurring biases or peculiar habits appear, expect these to influence his judgments of others. Use this as a diagnostic for likely partiality or systematic error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological consistency regarding experiment and observation
rubrics_metrics.description: If a critic regards physical 'axioms' as known only by observation and experiment, then where no observation or experiment is possible, no physical truth can be established — yet the critic must not claim validity for judgements about unperceived forces when his method denies such warrant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that the critic applies his methodological principles consistently (e.g., does he insist on experimental justification for some claims but accept analogous claims in unobservable domains?). Flag contradictions where methods are invoked selectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid internal contradictions in definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions and characterizations offered by a critic must be reconcilable — e.g., saying first that 'force' is that which changes the state of a body and later that 'force is the rate at which an agent does work per unit of length' introduces a contradiction: force as an agent vs force as a rate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a critic offers multiple definitions or formulations, demand reconciliation or coherence. Point out logical incompatibilities and ask for clarification or a unified concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect the necessity of abstract language for general laws
rubrics_metrics.description: In proportion as scientific terms express wider generalities, they necessarily lose that vividness of suggestion which words of concrete meanings have; the expression of highly abstract truths necessitates highly abstract words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dismiss abstract or technical formulations as meaningless merely because they seem vague to the uninitiated. Evaluate whether the abstraction is appropriate to the generality claimed; use examples to bridge comprehension rather than mockery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not strip technical terms into crude paraphrases that destroy meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Transforming abstract technical words into uncouth plain-English equivalents (e.g., 'homogeneity' → 'all-alikeness', 'differentiations' → 'somethingelseifications') can make legitimate statements appear nonsensical by losing the original scope and precision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of jargon should preserve the concept's range; avoid caricaturing specialized terms by crude literal substitutions. If translating, ensure the plain-language equivalent truly captures the technical sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish intrinsic from extrinsic absurdity
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a great difference between disclosing the absurdities contained in a thing and piling absurdities upon it; some minds are incapable of distinguishing between intrinsic absurdity and extrinsic absurdity (adventitious associations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When showing that a claim is absurd, separate what is intrinsically false in the idea from accidental, associative, or rhetorical causes of perceived absurdity (e.g., odd wording or cultural associations). Avoid attributing absurdity to the object when it arises from extrinsic dressing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid piling absurdities and associative fallacies
rubrics_metrics.description: Careful criticism exposes existing faults; careless or malicious criticism piles additional absurdities on the object under critique by means of incongruous juxtapositions or associative tricks (e.g., clothing an idea in ludicrous words to make the idea seem ludicrous).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from using associative effects (odd wording, metaphorical dressings) to make a doctrine appear absurd. Focus on the doctrine's substantive reasoning and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use current editions and accurate citations
rubrics_metrics.description: A conscientious critic usually consults the latest edition of the work he criticises, so that the author may have the benefit of any corrections or alterations he has made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify edition and textual basis before criticizing. Avoid quoting from obsolete editions when errors may have been corrected; failing to do so is an avoidable lapse in scholarship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match analytic methods to subject-matter competence
rubrics_metrics.description: Analytical faculties of one kind may be constantly exercised without strengthening analytical faculties of another kind — how mathematical analysis may be daily practiced without any skill in psychological analysis being acquired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the critic's habitual training equips him for the kind of analysis required (e.g., mathematical/formal skill does not guarantee insight into psychological or literary matters). Point out overreach when a critic applies unfamiliar modes of thought inappropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use examples pedagogically rather than to scoff
rubrics_metrics.description: When abstract formulae seem vague to the uninitiated, examples and concrete illustration can bring them within comprehension; mocking the abstraction without attempting to teach is unhelpful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer explanatory examples to ridicule. If an audience fails to grasp an abstract axiom, show it by a simple instance (as with a 'rustic' and Newton's laws) rather than deriding the abstract language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of and disclose personal bias or temperament
rubrics_metrics.description: A critic's temperament, jealousies, and personal peculiarities (e.g., a tendency to litigiousness, envy, or a preference for concealment) can distort his judgments; these traits often manifest across his writings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probe a critic's personal dispositions where relevant and note how these might skew interpretations. Require critics to separate personal grievances or affective motives from impartial assessment.
